title: We’ll Miss the Assistants When They’re Gone
text:
T he executive assistants are being laid off. According to Bloomberg , firms such as PwC and McKinsey have cut thousands of assistant and other support-staff positions. From the start of 2023 until the summer of 2025, openings for entry-level jobs typically requiring at least some college dropped by 35 percent . What executive needs a 23-year-old with student loans and big dreams when they can use a personal AI assistant to manage their calendars and book their flights for free?

 You might think that this position is a perfect candidate for robot replacement. If AI can do mindless administrative tasks as well as any human, then all that’s left is the emotional labor, which can be heavy—managing the hyperspecific preferences and enormous egos of entitled corporate titans. Get rid of this position, and businesses would save money while young people would—perhaps—find less humiliating jobs.

 But I spent almost two years as an executive assistant, and one of the many things I learned was that no one—not even the bosses who might want to replace us—had any sense of what we actually did.

 These positions play an important role in the job market, providing a rare entry point into competitive fields. Executive assistants run last-minute errands. They steer their bosses away from annoying people at dinner parties and memorize faces and relationship histories. They know their boss’s intimate secrets and how to anticipate their needs. They put out fires before the boss smells smoke. They serve as office managers, nannies, baristas, and human encyclopedias. The better an assistant is at their job, in other words, the less anyone knows what they do all day. And when they’re gone, we’re really going to miss them.

 I f you ask executive assistants what they think about being replaced by AI, they might say that they welcome a robot taking over chores like filing expenses, but that they can’t imagine handing over the trickier parts of their job. Maguire Grace Amundsen was Kylie Jenner’s executive assistant for more than two years. She’s now a sort of girlboss influencer, and is starting an interview series with high-powered women called Hot Commodities . Being a good executive assistant, she told me, requires understanding “a lot that is not said.” You have to know “the person that you’re working for in a way where even if they don’t say something, you kind of know what they’re saying.”

 You have to understand their every mood. One woman, who used to be an executive assistant to a famous fashion designer and his chief marketing officer, and asked to remain anonymous because she had signed an NDA, said that if the designer “was in a good mood, it’s fine to send the email asking if it’s okay that the car is not a Range Rover for Friday. But if he’s in a terrible mood, sending that is literally going to kill your day.”

 “AI can’t predict all that,” she told me. Companies would need to “hire a human assistant to handle the AI assistant.”

 [ Sophie Gilbert: The Assistant and the messes women clean up ] 

 Samantha, another former executive assistant, who asked me to use only her first name because she also signed an NDA, said that one of her most important roles was to serve as the scapegoat when anything went awry. She worked in the finance industry, and said a lot of her job was “taking the sword, and not taking that personally.” If something goes wrong anywhere in the company, you may be the one your boss yells at, and you get used to taking ownership for mistakes that weren’t your own.

 Samantha said she was privy to some of “the most intimate and personal things” in her bosses’ life: “colonoscopies, bonus sizes, who’s getting fired, who’s getting promoted, is divorce on the table.” The fashion assistant told me that the CMO’s “husband would call me. I talked to her driver. I talked to her hair stylist. I talked to her facialist. I talked to her kids. I talked to their school teachers.” At a time when most Americans distrust AI , it’s hard to imagine high-profile individuals wanting to share this kind of private information with a bot.

 But the more an executive assistant knows their boss, the more proactive they can be. High-powered executives often don’t have time to give instructions, and their assistants have to make judgment calls. “AI is really great at doing what you tell it to do, but a really good executive assistant is constantly thinking 345 steps ahead,” Samantha told me. “An EA needs to have the capacity to handle situations that don’t come with a clear set of instructions, whereas AI will always need a clear set of instructions.” Even if an executive theoretically fed an AI chatbot every bit of information (a big ask for someone who hires someone else to send their emails), there’s a level of nuance and emotional intelligence that you don’t get unless you are physically present in the room.

 Plus, most executives are looking to spend less time on their devices, not more. One of the main things assistants do is figure out what their boss actually needs to know from the onslaught of digital notifications and noise. “If you’re good at your job, you do a really great job of filtering, and I think that element would be lost,” Amundsen told me.

 To be fair, if you ask most anyone in most any field whether they think they can be replaced by AI, they’re likely to say absolutely not . But executive assistants have one more thing going for them: Perhaps the biggest reason executives like having them around is simply to flaunt them.

 “There is a level of prestige to having a dedicated assistant,” Anthony Taylor, an executive assistant at Hermès, told me. It’s how you know you’ve succeeded. He used to work at a smaller agency, where his old boss would bring him to events just to show that she was important enough to bring him to events. It’s the same reason that people send emails “looping my assistant in.”

 [ Annie Lowrey: How ChatGPT will destabilize white-collar work ] 

 “No one’s going to be impressed by the fact that you’re paying some subsidiary of Claude to manage your calendar and your emails,” Taylor said.

 For this reason, human assistants will probably continue to have a place in status-obsessed industries that want to signal their refined taste, if nowhere else. These assistants don’t just book cars; they make sure the driver is wearing the right outfit and carrying the right brand of mints. They don’t just book the restaurant; they book the impossible restaurant, the kind you can’t get into unless someone at the hospitality group that owns the whole establishment owes you a favor. They cultivate their own network of maître d’s and publicists, and when their boss brings them to an event, they’re a status symbol in flesh and blood.

 T ake away the assistants , and lots of executives would probably have meltdowns. But that’s not what worries me most.

 The position of executive assistant is especially valuable for young people with backgrounds like mine. I would probably not be writing for this magazine if I hadn’t landed a job as an executive assistant here in 2023. I came from the South, had no connections in journalism, and little experience in the field. What I did have was a master’s degree, a résumé full of odd jobs, and the willingness to take notes in meetings. Eventually, I elbowed my way off the business side of the magazine and into writing.

 My story is a common one for people who want to land jobs in competitive, creative industries, but don’t have the perfect résumé or connections. “I was very unequipped, network-wise, moving to the city and pursuing fashion in any capacity, especially fashion PR, which is notoriously insular and elitist,” Taylor, who was raised in Mississippi, told me. When Taylor, who’s now 25, first set out to move to New York, he scoured the internet for anyone who could help him get his foot in the door. “My first actual successful attempt at networking was I strategically went on a date with someone who I knew worked in the industry,” he told me. It worked—his résumé was sent to a few agencies. He got an unpaid internship for a few months, during which he “spent all of my savings trying to stay afloat.” Eventually, a communications-assistant position that involved working on brand accounts opened up. He applied, but the role was given to the daughter of an executive at a major fashion magazine. The executive-assistant job was his “consolation prize,” he said. It required humility, but it was his ticket into the industry.

 Some people say that everyone should have to work a service-industry job, because there are certain life lessons that can only be learned as a 19-year-old busing tables for snobby customers. My version of this argument is that everyone in corporate America should have to work as an assistant in their industry for a year. There are few jobs as frustrating and formative. You will learn to earn your keep. And if you’re as lucky as I was, you gain generous mentors who have successfully navigated the industry you want to be a part of.

 [ Matteo Wong & Charlie Warzel: AI agents are here. Nobody’s ready. ] 

 You learn resilience: to take blame when no fault is your own, to humble yourself, to take menial tasks seriously, to go overlooked and unthanked. You learn to make judgment calls and not need external validation to know you’ve done a good job. But most of all, being an executive assistant makes you learn people , which is the most valuable skill in almost any industry.

 Young people need proof that there’s still a ladder left to climb in corporate America, and that if they’re willing to start on the lowest rung, swallow their pride, and be someone’s executive assistant, they can make it to the top. So, long live the human executive assistant. May their days be plenty and may their bosses be pleased with them.

 And if the bosses can’t be pleased, let them have the satisfaction of yelling at a 20-something, instead of a screen.
